newsitem.title: UK: Official sales, disinvestment hurt gold price - GFMS.
newsitem.headline: Official sales, disinvestment hurt gold price - GFMS.

text.p: A rise in official sector sales was the chief cause of weakness in the gold price in the second half of 1996, Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS) said in a report.

Combined with disinvestment by the private sector, the official sector sales outweighed the impact of a recovery in physical demand in the latter half of last year, GFMS said in its Gold 1996-Update II, which was issued on Wednesday.
Supply from the official sector was estimated at 208 tonnes in 1996, an increase of 12.3 percent over the previous year.
Most of these sales from the second half of the year appeared to originate in Europe and totalled 123 tonnes.

The dollar price in the second half of the year drifted lower until a sharp drop in mid-November took gold to the lowest London PM fix of the year at $367.40, it noted. But the average price of $387.87 was marginally above the 1995 level.
Mine production was estimated up 2.9 percent at 2,328 tonnes, after two years of declines.
South African output fell by nearly 30 tonnes, but US producers halted recent output declines and Canadian and Australian producers posted notable increases.
Forward sales did not have a significant impact on the market overall but rose in the final quarter.
Total supply in the gold market was estimated at 3,432 tonnes, a decrease of 4.7 percent against 1995.
On the demand side, jewellery led a recovery in fabrication demand due to growth in India, consolidation of a first-half increase in the Middle East and a rebound in demand in the Far East.
But the investment scenario for gold was poor, illustrated by a 52.9 percent decline in bar hoarding and net physical disinvestment in Europe.
But dominating the scene was New York-based speculative short selling, the report said.
Gold's failure to hang on to the highs of the year, along with advances in the U.S. stockmarket and lack of inflationary pressures, contributed to poor sentiment towards gold.

Market sentiment was also bruised by fears of official sector selling linked to European Monetary Union criteria and concerns that producers would resume hedging after many companies let forward selling positions decline mid-year.

"The fourth quarter saw such views justified, with the physical market being unable to absorb the resulting quantities of gold emanating from official, disinvestment and hedging transactions," the update said.
In future, although the physical market looks healthy, the key to the level of gold prices may lie with the level of U.S. equity prices.

"If these continue to rise, then it is hard to see a sudden reversal of the speculative short selling which was responsible for pushing the price down recently," the update said, quoting GFMS chief executive Stewart Murray.
"On the other hand, were the rise in share prices to be perceived as seriously over-extended, then gold might be one of the few beneficiaries," he added.
